A lowland species found mainly below 200 m elevation, which is certainly true of known Australian populations, but it has been recorded from 0--1500 m elevation across its range. Typically found on sandy to clay soils along watercourses, along the margins of swamps and in seasonally wet savannahs in fully exposed to moderately shaded situations. It typically favours drier situations than N. rowaniae and N. tenax where the species co-occur, whereas in various parts of Southeast Asia it has been documented growing in permanent bodies of shallow water. High elevation populations are more typically observed in large mountain complexes or upland plateaus as a result of the Massenerhebung (mountain mass) effect, which sees warmer conditions manifested at higher elevations (A. Robinson, pers. obs).

Prior to 2005, all recent revisions of Nepenthes maintained Danser’s (1928) broad interpretation of N. mirabilis in Australia, however, these revisions were undertaken with no documented study of materials held at Australia’s major herbaria, in particularly BRI, or indeed of plants growing in situ to formally document any ecological differences between the proposed taxa (Clarke & Kruger 2005), as well as the degree of reproductive isolation that they might exhibit. Occurs as a component of coastal vegetation from Carnarvon to Perth in Western Australia and from E of Albany in Western Australia to Portland in Victoria; also in inland South Australia, western Victoria and western New South Wales. There are isolated records from the Northern Territory and Queensland, which may represent introductions through agricultural activities.

Clearance of Nitraria billardierei for control of feral species is often a controversial subject. It has been allowed in some parts of South Australia under State legislation but permission still needs to be sought from the Native Vegetation Council. Leaves and inflorescences often have gall-like infestations and these may well prove of interest since gall-forming armoured scale insects (Diaspidiotus species) have been documented on Nitraria species elsewhere (E.M. Danzig, J. Zoosyst. Rossica 8: 287--289 (1999). Similarly, the sphecid wasps Solierella nitraria Pulawski and Cerceris nitrariae Morice (R.M. Bohart & A.S. Menke, Sphecid wasps of the world: a generic revision (1976)) described from Egypt and Morocco respectively, were named for their association with Nitraria species and it would be interesting to see whether these same associations occur in Australian populations. The fruits of Nitraria billardierei are edible and particularly attractive to emus, and possibly to rock-parrots (S.A. White, Emu 16: 1--15 (1916)), but are also taken by kangaroos, sheep, rabbits, lizards and decorator ants; germination was found to be enhanced after passage through an emu (J.C. Noble, J. Ecol. 63: 979--984 (1975)). N. billardierei fruits have also been recorded as part of the diet of Australian Aborigines (B. Gott, Telopea 12: 215--226 (2008)) and have been eaten without any ill effects by the author. They have potential for development as a native food, although a little salty. Possibly not distinct from the Russian species Nitraria schoberi. While there is a documented chromosome number difference (2n = 24 for N. schoberi and 2n = 48 for N. billardierei), morphological differences, including spininess and leaf and floral characteristics, have not been investigated fully. Morphological differences, including habit and size of the stones, were documented by Noble & Whalley (1978a) between the populations of Nitraria billardierei occurring along the Indian Ocean and those which occur along the Southern Ocean. Again, a molecular study across the range of the species could prove useful, particularly given the expanding distribution in inland areas.

There is conflicting information on this species. The seeds are reported to be mucilaginous on wetting but those which were observed showed no evidence of any mucilaginous substances. Instead, the outer reticulately-marked surface expanded, apparently trapping a great deal of air between it and the embryo. Seeds also yield a dye called “Turkey Red” used for colouring tarbooshes (Mabberley 1987: 437) and for dyeing carpets in Turkey and Iran (Emboden 1972) but other references within dyeing books also attribute the dye known by this name to Madder (Rubia tinctorum). The colour of the dye extracted from the seeds depends on whether the extraction is done in water (yellow fluorescent) or alcohol (red). Peganum harmala plants have an unpleasant smell and are possibly poisonous to livestock. The alkaloids contained within the roots and seeds possibly account for this, as they may also account for a number of reputed medicinal properties ranging from emetic to antispasmodic, narcotic, stimulant and antihelminthic (Ghafoor 1977: 9). Emboden (1972) also refers to the aphrodisiac, narcotic and hallucinogenic properties of Peganum harmala. The properties of Peganum harmala are also provided by Parsons & Cuthbertson (2001: 637--639).

It is possible that the Australasian populations are not conspecific with those found in Europe, but no attempt was made to determine this. Mr William Archer (pers. comm.), who has made a study of this species, found that over 90% of a population reappeared each year even though they may have had their fronds eaten by animals or collected in the previous season. Within populations, the size of the plants can vary considerably and extremely small plants may produce a frond a few centimetres long. In such small plants the fertile sporophore is simple, with the sporangia in 2 rows; however, there are usually paired sporangia at the base of the sporophore. The pinnae are also variable within populations. Thus, although they usually have entire or slightly irregular margins, these are occasionally prominently crenulate and often have 1 medial or a number of incisions dissecting the pinnae. This latter situation appears to correlate with very robust plants. Very rarely up to 3 fertile sporophores may arise on a frond, each with its own stipe. I have also observed the occasional plant of B. australe to produce a second fertile sporophore.

Flowers exposed to the sun are pollinated by a small stingless bee, Tetragonula carbonaria, which, with extended mouthparts, forces its way to base of labellum (Jones 1981). The bee probes the calli and labellum sac for about 30 seconds before backing out, often receiving the orchid’s pollinarium on the thorax. After emergence from the flower, the insect cleans its antennae, mouthparts and front legs assiduously as if collecting an important compound. The fragrant flowers last less than day, opening early in morning and often finishing by midday. Sections of flowers on the racemes open simultaneously in spasms and generally all the plants in an area flower at same time, known as synchronous flowering or massed gregarious flowering. The whole area becomes saturated with a spicy perfume which stimulates local insects and allows the orchids to compete successfully for their attention. Tetragonula carbonaria also pollinates Pomatocalpa macphersonii, this time picking up the orchid pollinarium on the head. Flowers in the shade are uncommonly pollinated.

The flowers open fully during day and partially close at night with the tepals incurving over the column and labellum. The flowers last 1--3 days and have a fruity fragrance that specifically attracts male fruit flies of the genus Bactrocera (order Diptera, family Tephrotidae); 2 common native species are B. jarvisi and B. tryoni. These male fruit flies do not attempt to mate with the flowers but instead feed in the flower and take in chemical components of the floral fragrance which are vital for specific aspects of the insect’s sex life and reproduction (Tan & Nishida 2007). The flies visit the flowers in the morning and probe the sepals and petals, eventually feeding on the labellum which tips when the point of balance is passed trapping the insect against the column. While attempting to retreat the fly becomes stuck firmly in the viscidium, sometimes for more than 30 minutes, all the while struggling until eventually it frees itself with the pollinarium attached to its back. Pollination occurs when the insect visits another flower. See also Teck et al. (2011). Sometimes the insect perishes after becoming trapped in the flower (Smythe 1969, personal observations).

Widespread and common, particularly in coastal lowlands, but also extending to high elevations in ranges and tablelands. In some areas it extends to the western slopes of the Dividing Range. It forms strands and large masses on trees, boulders and cliff faces in mangroves, coastal forests, rainforests and humid areas of open forest in shady or exposed, sunny situations.
Qld (NE: Moa Island in the Torres Strait, Cape York to Paluma Ranges); 5--1200 m altitude; also occurs in New Guinea and Irian Jaya.

Plants produce inflorescences over 4--6 weeks during the wet season. All the flowers on an inflorescence mature and open together. They release a light, fruity perfume in periods of warm, humid weather. Nectar is produced in large droplets and coalesces in the base of the labellum. A pollination study in Atherton, Qld, using cultivated plants of this species, originally obtained from the McIlwraith Range on Cape York Peninsula, showed that the fly Silba excelsa (order Diptera, family Lonchaeidae) was attracted to the flowers to feed on nectar (Jones & Gray 1975). The flies feed on nectar on the labellum, moving into the flower until the labellum tilts, trapping the fly between the labellum and the stelidia on the column. The fly struggles and backs out of the flower, picking up the pollinarium on its thorax. Pollen is transferred to the stigma of another flower on a subsequent visit.

Australian populations of this orchid have been decimated by over-collecting. It is one of a group of species, distributed across countries in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, which have very similar flowers displayed in a horizontal semicircle at the end of a long, slender stalk. Although of similar general form, the flowers also display individual patterns of colour which have most likely evolved within regional habitats to attract specific pollinators. This complex group of taxa has been interpreted in various ways by different authorities.

The relatively large flowers release a strong, unusual scent that smells like semen or fish meal. Nectar, exuded in large droplets, coalesces in the labellum groove and also flows into small pouches formed by the lateral sepals. The scent is very noticeable on warm days and attracts blowflies of genus Calliphora (family Calliphoridae), particularly C. tibialis, which actively work the flowers and feed on the nectar. The labellum tip is at first outwards as the fly feeds, but as the fly moves forwards the labellum eventually tips inwards and traps fly between the column and labellum. The fly buzzes furiously while trapped, eventually picking up pollinarium on its thorax. Pollen is transferred to the broad, sticky stigma of another flower on a subsequent visit. For details of pollination see Jones (1985).

The flowers have a sweet, musky scent and attract male short-tongue bees, Leioproctus obscurus (family Colletidae), apparently by sexual deceit (see Kuiter 2014). Normally these bees feed on nectar in native legumes, but Caladenia rosella is nectarless. Only male bees have been seen on the orchid flowers and they approach downwind as if following a scent trail. Pseudocopulatory movements have been observed when the bees are on the labellum. Male bees emerge earlier than female bees in their life cycle and the flowering time of the orchid may exploit this numerical disparity of the sexes. Details on ecology also provided by Carr (1988: 445).

The orchid grows in small, sparse, clonal colonies, sometimes close to the base of trees. It flowers freely without fire, but flowering is promoted when dense habitats are burnt. It is also often seen flowering in mowed or slashed areas. Usually only 1 or 2 flowers are open at any time. The flowers are sturdy and quite long-lived, lasting for several weeks if not pollinated or burnt by bushfires. In dry seasons the leaves are often withered by the time flowering takes place. The final flowers of the season, which open towards the end of spring, survive well into summer if conditions are amenable. Flowers have even been recorded as late as May, a six-month flowering period (Jones 1970). Remarkably these plants were flowering alongside the emerged leaves of the next generation. Patience is needed when studying the pollination of Caleana major, as insect visitation is meagre in natural populations and insects are not readily attracted to flowers placed out during baiting studies. A couple of reports showed that the flowers of C. major attracted the attention of male sawflies which become effectively trapped between the triggered labellum and the column. The sawflies were identified as Lophyrotoma leachii (Cady 1965) from observations made at Narooma, N.S.W.; and a species of Pterygophorus (Bates 1989) near Wauchope, N.S.W. Photographs of four species of Lophyrotoma trapped in the flowers and/or carrying pollinia are presented in Kuiter (2016, page 111 and 2017). Identified as L. interrupta, L. nigripes, L. ramosa and L. zonalis, these images clearly show the sawfly on the labellum with its head held close to the beak, or trapped headfirst between the labellum and column. Sexual deception most likely plays a role in the pollination of this species and at least one image in Kuiter 2017 shows a male sawfly standing on the beak of the ducks-head labellum with its abdomen apparently probing the head in a pseudocopulatory posture. Further research is obviously needed to determine the number of sawfly species involved in the pollination of C. major. The flowers of C. major can be very long-lived (6--10 weeks) and successful pollination is rare. Indeed, the pioneering Australian orchid botanist R.D. Fitzgerald records seeing no insect visits and only 4 capsules developing in a population of 127 flowers that he monitored in 1878 near Sydney. By comparison, Caleana minor is much more frequently pollinated and commonly produces capsules. For more details on Caleana major pollination see Bower 2001: 141--143.

Flowering occurs regularly in open habitats, and is enhanced by summer fires in dense habitats. At Mullion Creek, N.S.W., Caleana minor is pollinated by males of a completely black species of thynnine wasp, Thynnoturneria armiger (Bower 2014), whereas in parts of Vic. species of Neozeleboria are actively involved (Kuiter 2016). Further research is needed over the natural range of C. minor to clarify details of its pollination in different regions and habitats and the possible involvement of cryptic species (both in the orchid and the wasps). The males of other species of thynnine wasp may also be attracted to the flowers of C. minor (Bower 1992, 2007; Bower & Brown 2009) because of similar, but not identical, sex pheromones (see Kuiter 2016, 2017; Kuiter & Findlater-Smith 2018). Apomixis is known to occur in C. minor (Clements 1995). All plants in S.A. are apparently totally apomictic, attracting no pollinating insects, the ovaries swelling even before the flowers open and becoming quite swollen and turgid early in anthesis (Bates 1984, Bates & Weber 1990, Bates 2006). By contrast the ovaries of non-apomictic C. minor are not swollen in early flower and the flowers usually attract wasps for pollination. Freak variants of C. minor in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. and around the Grampians in western Vic. are able to reproduce by apomixis. These freaks, which form small, localised patches in some areas, have abortive labella which cannot function normally and malformed columns and anthers which may or may not contain pollen.

Widespread and often locally common; frequently growing in open sites on forested ridges and slopes among litter and shrubs in freely draining clay loam, stony loam and gravelly soil. It also occurs in coastal scrub and heath in leached sand and under sheoaks in stony soil, rarely in moss and lichen pads on granite rocks. At some sites it grows in exposed patches of quartz or quartzite chips and colonises disturbed sites such as track margins, old quarries and gravel scrapes. In New Zealand it grows in litter and moss under shrubs near geothermally active ground.

2 apomictic variants have been formally named as distinct species. The first, described by Baron von Mueller as Caleya sullivanii in 1882, was based on specimens collected by D. Sullivan in January of that year from near Mt Zero in the southern Grampians, western Vic. It was transferred to Caleana in 1926 and then placed in Paracaleana in 1972. This freak apomictic variant also occurs nearby at Dadswells Bridge where a study showed that plants of P. sullivanii were interspersed with morphologically distinct and apparently normal plants of Caleana minor (Jones 1977). The same study also revealed the extreme aberrant morphology of P. sullivanii. For example, the labellum laminae ranged from a modified structure with only a slight resemblance to the labellum of C. minor, to flat, petaloid, non-glandular structures with no obvious similarities. Additionally the abortive labellum strap was immobile or capable of only slight movement and often the sepals, petals and column were ornamented haphazardly with labellum calli. The column was reduced in size and of a very different shape to a normal column, and the anther was abortive or completely absent. Difference in these abortive features were also found between individual flowers on a single inflorescence, indicating the high degree of instability in the floral morphology. The second freak to be named at species rank was Caleana nublingii which was described by the Victorian orchid botanist W.H. Nicholls in 1931 based on plants collected by Erwin Nubling in 1930 from Bell in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. Plants and flowers of both these freak taxa are illustrated by colour plates in Nicholls (1969) - P. sullivanii on Plate 176 and C. nublingii on plate 177.

Pollinated by an undescribed species of scoliid wasp which was photographed by Bruce Gray while it was attempting to mate with the orchid’s labellum (Jones & Gray (1974); photo in Jones (2021: 33). So strong was the attraction that the wasps appeared within minutes of placing a cut inflorescence in the sunlight. Up to 30 wasps have been captured in a day after being attracted to a solitary inflorescence. Sometimes 3 or 4 wasps converge on a single flower, fighting and scrambling for possession. If the flowers are covered, the wasps are still attracted and land on the cover, seeking the flowers. The approach of insects to the flowers is rapid and direct. They land on the labellum with their head near the column and make copulatory movements with the abdomen. The head contacts the friable pollen, dislodging some onto the stigma and a significant amount sticks on the head for transport to another flower.

Chiloglottis cornuta is the most widely distributed species in the genus. The flowers are self-pollinating. In some areas the flowers open freely and have widely spreading lateral sepals and petals and a protruding labellum, often held nearly horizontally. This variant occasionally crosses with C. valida, presumably when the pollinator mistakenly visits the wrong flower. In other areas the flowers do not open widely, sometimes hardly at all, the segments mostly remain incurved and the labellum remains obliquely erect. The labellum calli are extremely variable in number, size, shape (mounded, flat, linear or ridge-like) and colour (green, reddish or black). Calli are occasionally fused into ridge-like structures.

Widespread and often locally common, extending from the coast in some areas (King Island.) to high in the mountains. Found growing among shrubs, ferns, moss colonies and deep forest litter in shady, humid, sheltered sites in tall, moist to wet forest, including wet sclerophyll forest dominated by mountain ash, rainforest dominated by myrtle beech, streamside vegetation, fern gullies and coastal scrub in freely draining to moisture-retentive loam; plants occasionally grow in shallow running water. It also colonises litter on boulders, rotting logs, living and dead tree fern trunks and sphagnum mounds in subalpine areas. In S.A. it grows in bogs with sphagnum and ferns.

S.A. (Nangwarry in SE), N.S.W. (rare in SE, Snowy Mountains), Vic. (mainly in E & NE, scattered and uncommon in W including the Grampians), Tas. (widespread, King Island, Flinders Island); 50--2000 m altitude; also occurs in New Zealand and Campbell Islands.

The original specimen used to describe Chiloglottis trilabra was a freak peloric flower that had three labella. This species, together with Cryptostylis subulata, Diplodium alatum and Eriochilus cucullatus, was among the earliest Australian orchids to be scientifically described. It was first collected in 1793 by a group of French botanists and biologists, headed by Jacques-Julien Houtou de Labillardière who named the species in 1806 as Epipactis reflexa. These scientists, who were on a French expedition which visited south-eastern Tas. while searching for the lost expedition of La Pérouse, collected around Recherche Bay for five weeks between January and May 1793. The botanical results of the collections, including illustrations, were published in two volumes entitled Nova Hollandiae Plantarum Specimen in 1804--1806. Epipactis reflexa was illustrated on tab. 211 in the second volume. The type specimens and/or original illustrations of Labillardière’s Australian orchids are housed in the Herbarium at the University of Florence in Italy.

Exhibits variation in size and shape of flowers and prominence of labellum boss. Flower colour ranges from reddish purple to dark purple (almost black), with the depth of the colour impacting on the prominence of the stripes on the edges of the labellum. The central boss on the labellum varies in size, prominence (flat to strongly mounded) and colour (white to greenish or suffused with purple). Size and shape of marginal teeth on labellum also varies, from short and broad, to long and narrow with blunt to sharp points. Sometimes these variations can be seen within a small area, but are more often observed in different habitats and soil types. Bishop (1996) draws attention to a variant from coastal areas of western Vic. and S.A. which has spreading or recurved labellum margins and longer-than-usual auricles. This has been treated as Corybas dilatatus by some authorities. Jeanes & Backhouse (2006) include a photo of an unusual variant from near Portland with pale pinkish red flowers, a large, pale boss and a labellum with very shortly toothed margins.

A detailed study provides interesting details of this highly specialised species (Gibson 1994). It grows and flowers in summer, producing stolonoid roots and daughter tubers which are dormant over winter, sprouting in late spring as new plants. Although plants occur up to c. 150 m elevation, most flowering plants are found below 50 m elevation. It has friable pollen and is probably self-pollinating since a high proportion of flowers produce fruit. Seeds are shed in early March; capsules of some plants, but apparently not all, arise on an extended, fleshy peduncle c. 40 mm above the ground. It is also recorded that feral rabbits (now gone from the island) did not eat the orchid leaves.

Widespread, but disjunct and mainly localised in coastal and near-coastal areas. Found growing in a range of moist to wet habitats, including seepage sites in sparsely treed, dense, shrubby heathland and swamps, often in association with stunted plants of scented paperbark and grasstrees, in black peaty soil. In wet habitats, it commonly grows on tops of small mounds and corrugations, and within tussocks of spiky rushes. The areas become filled with water after heavy rain and the orchid plants can be totally submerged for a period. In the subtropics this species grows in wetlands dominated by broad-leaved paperbark (Melaleuca quinquenervia). A disjunct montane population occurs at high altitude on Timbarra Plateau, northern N.S.W., growing with Baeckea omissa (Lachlan Copeland pers. comm.).

S.A. (Yundi Swamp on Fleurieu Peninsula), Qld (Maaroom, Noosa, Burleigh Heads, Tugun), N.S.W. (Brunswick Heads to Wonboyn, inland at Timbarra Plateau at 960m altitude), Vic. (scattered disjunctly in S from E to W), Tas. (Flinders Island); 0--960 m altitude.

In recently burnt areas the flowers are often quite large by comparison with the leaf, sometimes even twice the size of the supporting leaf. Corybas unguiculatus sometimes grows close to C. fordhamii, often in well-drained soil on the drier margins of swamps. C. unguiculatus finishes flowering 2--3 weeks before C. fordhamii starts to flower. Variation within C. fordhamii needs further study. Plants from western Vic. have smaller, more boldly striped flowers than those further east. A small population from S.A. is quite distinct morphologically from populations in eastern states and probably represents an undescribed species. It has pale reddish flowers with a broadly tapered, less-bulbous dorsal sepal, a strongly inflated labellum with a very wide opening subtended by a broad, protruding beak and larger openings on the auricles. It is known from a single swamp where it is now extremely rare or possibly extinct due to human interference, changes in hydrology and weed growth.

This orchid can be very difficult to see when growing among dense, tussocky vegetation. Flowering is inhibited in the first year or two after a fire. Cryptostylis hunteriana is an obligate mycoheterotrophic orchid that is associated with saprophytic fungi and decaying wood for its carbon source and nutrition. It is an opportunistic species that often appears as small, slender, few-flowered individuals, most of which only last one season before dying. By contrast, plants which have achieved a suitable symbiotic relationship with a mycorrhizal fungus are vigorous and multiflowered. Small, closely placed tufts of plants may be the result of localised vegetative reproduction or seedlings developing close to their parents. Tagged plants studied by Mark Clements revealed an interesting pattern of development. Small plants growing in less than ideal microhabitats generally die after flowering, having used all the energy stored in their small rhizome. Larger plants often did not flower in the following season. Natural pollination rates were low, only 1--2% of the flowers producing capsules. Laboratory experiments showed that seedling development was very rapid, with rhizomes growing over 3 cm long within eight months of sowing, suggesting that plants may be large enough to flower within 18 months of seed germination.

Commonly found growing on bloodwoods (Corymbia species) and hard-barked species of Eucalyptus, such as ironbarks, boxes and smooth-barked gums, several species of which make a perfect host for the orchid by providing hollows with central pipelines of decaying heartwood in the trunk, and larger branches on which plants can establish. The extensive roots and rhizome systems of this orchid extend deep into the decaying heartwood of the host tree (sometimes to the base of the tree), the rhizomes emerging as new growths from other hollows to form new clumps several metres away from the original clump. The long roots, large tough pseudobulbs adapted for moisture storage, and thick channelled leaves which direct any rain into the root system, are important factors that enable these hardy orchids to survive in areas of low and intermittent rainfall. The decaying heartwood that retains moisture after rain also aids their survival. Apart from species of Corymbia and Eucalyptus, this orchid also grows on species of Angophora (A. floribunda, A. melanoxylon), long-lived wattles such as Acacia salicina, native pines, kurrajong and buloke. These orchids flower freely in most seasons, but in some years they may produce massed floral displays.

This is probably Australia’s best known native orchid. It is very popular in cultivation and has been widely used in hybridisation. German orchid specialist Heinrich Gustav Reichenbach records this orchid as being cultivated at Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, England, in 1824 (Reichenbach 1878), but it was not described formally until 1852. The British botanist John Lindley based his description on plants collected from Mt Adolphus Island, a small island c. 18 km north-east of Cape York. These plants were collected by Dr John Thomson, surgeon on HMS Rattlesnake which was on an exploratory voyage of northern Australia and New Guinea during 1846--1850 and was in Torres Strait late in 1849 (Macgillivray 1852, Lavarack 2013). The large, colourful flowers apparently attracted much attention in England and probably added impetus to local nurseries to send paid collectors to new areas seeking commercial quantities of this species and other exotic specimens. Interest was also displayed by botanists of the time, such as John Lindley and Heinrich Reichenbach, looking for new species to name. 2 London nurseries in particular, J.H. Veitch & Sons and Victoria and Paradise Nurseries received ‘quantities’ of living plants of D. bigibbum (probably hundreds of plants, perhaps even thousands) from their respective collectors, John Veitch and Andrew Goldie. Veitch collected plants from Mt Adolphus Island in 1865 and subsequently a plant from this collection with large flowers was named Dendrobium bigibbum var. superbum by Reichenbach in 1878. This large-flowered variant was from the same small island where the type specimen of D. bigibbum was collected. Goldie collected from an undisclosed island in Torres Strait in 1876 and a white-flowered plant from this collection was named D. bigibbum var. candidum by Reichenbach in 1878. Plants of D. bigibbum have been extensively collected from the wild, but the species is still common in most areas and has the ability to rapidly recolonise sites from which it has been over-collected. Hybridises with D. discolor (see D. ×superbiens).

In very dry seasons, the plants can shed all their leaves before commencing new growth. Bruce Gray collected 2 species of native bee carrying pollinia and visiting the flowers of cultivated plant of Dendrobium canaliculatum at Atherton, north-eastern Qld, in October 1971. The bees were identified as Hylaeus ruficeps and H. theodorei in the family Colletidae. Bartareau (1995) studied the pollination of D. canaliculatum (cited as Dendrobium canaliculatum var. nigrescens) and D. tattonianum (cited as Dendrobium canaliculatum var. canaliculatum) and observed 2 species of Hylaeus, namely H. chromaticus and H. ruficeps, removing pollinia and pollinating flowers. He concluded that the bees were attracted by floral fragrance and not colour and there was no pollinator discrimination between the 2 orchid taxa. He also observed that the bees spend at least 10 minutes in a flower, scratching and chewing on the calli and base of the labellum.

Hybridises rarely with Dendrobium johannis and D. discolor. Dendrobium canaliculatum, together with D. rigidum and D. undulatum (D. discolor), was first collected in Australia by British naturalist Joseph Banks in 1770 at Endeavour River. Banks, together with the Swedish naturalist Daniel Solander, was one of the scientists on board Captain Cook’s barque Endeavour when it was careened on the bank of what is now the Endeavour River (in the vicinity of present day Cooktown, north-eastern Qld) after a damaging encounter with coral on the Great Barrier Reef. Scottish botanist Robert Brown used the Banks’ collection as the type when he described Dendrobium canaliculatum in 1810.

Hybridises with Dendrobium nindii, D. biggibum and D. johannis. An unusual aberrant variant was described as Dendrobium elongatum by H.M.R. Rupp in 1953 based on 4 plants collected in 1952 by Stanley F. Goessling-St Cloud growing on a tree of Dillenia alata in the mangrove scrub of Trinity Inlet, Cairns, Qld. The flowers had unusually narrow, tapered segments which did not twist and the labellum lacked lateral lobes. A cultivated plant, however subsequently produced a raceme of flowers typical of D. discolor. This species, together with Dendrobium canaliculatum and D. rigidum, was first collected in Australia by Swedish naturalist Dr Daniel Carl Solander in 1770. Solander was one of the scientists on board Captain Cook’s barque Endeavour and he, together with Joseph Banks, collected this orchid at 4 locations on the Qld coast: Bustard Bay (Seventeen Seventy), Bay of Inlets (Thirsty Sound near Shoalwater Bay), Cape Grafton (Mission Bay near Cairns), and later at the Endeavour River (in the vicinity of present day Cooktown, Qld) where the ship was careened after a damaging encounter with coral on the Great Barrier Reef. The orchid was named Dendrobium undulatum by Scottish botanist Robert Brown in 1810, but the name was invalid having been used previously in 1807 by the Dutch mycologist Christiaan Hendrik Persoon. The English botanist John Lindley redescribed the species as D. discolor in 1841 using a cultivated plant originally collected in the East Indies.

The strongly scented flowers are produced in abundance on large plants and are pollinated by small native bees of the genus Homalictus in the family Halictidae (Jones & Gray 1977). The flowers release a heavy, spicy perfume during the mornings of warm days, this scent becoming strongest mid-morning, and barely detectable by midday. Most insect visits occur during the mornings. The insect enters the flower through a tube formed by the large lateral lobes of the labellum where they embrace the column. The bee probes the base of the flower, particularly a small, dark, sunken, moist spot at the base of the column foot. Glue from the rostellum is smeared on the thorax of the insect as it enters the flower and when it backs out from the flower, hairs on its thorax catch on the anther cap causing it to pivot and eject the pollinia onto the smeared patch. The bee is only inside the flower for 10--30 seconds before leaving. Pollen deposition occurs during a visit to another flower when the pollinia catches in the stigma, which narrows upwards. After a brief struggle by the insect, the pollinia becomes detached in the stigma.

This is a variable species; plants from lowland areas tend to have slender pseudobulbs and small, white flowers fairly well spaced on the racemes, whereas those from higher elevations in ranges and tablelands have stouter pseudobulbs, thicker leathery leaves and larger crowded flowers. The taxon known as Dendrobium fusiforme var. blackburnii was first named in 1950 by W.H. Nicholls based on a plant cultivated by him and originally collected by J.A. Blackburn in 1945 from Font Hills south of Mt Carbine, Qld. It purportedly differed from Dendrobium jonesii by its robust pseudobulbs (120--220 × 25--30 mm), pendulous racemes and small yellow flowers with short blunt segments. This mysterious taxon has not been relocated since the original collection and remains poorly known. Its flowers are smaller and quite different in form and colour to the spidery white flowers of typical D. jonesii, but an illustration of its labellum shows a similar truncate apex on the midlobe (see plate 397, Nicholls 1969).

Within this species there is a general trend for plants from south-eastern Qld to have longer pseudobulbs than those from the southern part of its range in N.S.W. This orchid is however, extremely variable in a number of features, including length and thickness of pseudobulbs, propensity to form aerial growths, leaf size, shape and colour, flower colour, texture, and width of floral segments. Even within a localised area a significant range of variation can be found. Hundreds of selections have been collected and grown by orchid enthusiasts. The superior types with good flower size, colour, shape and propensity to flower, are sold or traded as clones, frequently under a cultivar name. The following named varieties have no botanical standing, but are of significance to horticulturists: Dendrobium kingianum var. pallidum has pale to white flowers; D. kingianum var. silcockii has white flowers with colourful, dark pink-purple markings on the labellum; D. kingianum var. aldersoniae has long pseudobulbs and bright pink flowers on long racemes; D. kingianum var. pulcherrimum has short, stubby pseudobulbs, bluish green, greyish or silvery leaves, short, few-flowered racemes and largish, pink to mauve flowers - It forms crowded, compact clumps on rocks in relatively exposed situations between Kempsey and Bulahdelah in N.S.W.

Pollinated by female worker bees in the genus Tetragonula (formerly Trigona) (Bartareau 1994) visiting the flowers on warm, windless afternoons. The flowers are nectarless and produce a sweet perfume on warm to hot days. The bees sometimes hover in front of the flowers or move from flower to flower on the raceme. On entering the flower they receive a coating of sticky stigmatic fluid on the thorax and spend 20--30 minutes scratching close to the base of the column or labellum, with the tight angle of the labellum holding the insect against the column. While struggling to exit the flower, pollinia are deposited on the sticky patch smeared on the insect’s thorax. Deposition on the stigma occurs when visiting a second flower.

The growth habit of plants is maintained in cultivation and a short-growing coastal variant produces masses of aerial growths and flowers poorly compared with the taller upland variant. Australian surveyor and orchid botanist Robert David Fitzgerald collected Dendrobium moorei on a visit to Lord Howe Island in 1869 in company with Charles Moore. He later prepared an excellent plate of the orchid accompanied by the following text. ‘It was named by Baron Mueller, in honour of C. Moore, Director of the Botanic Gardens, Sydney, from specimens I procured at Howe’s Island in 1869, where I again obtained it in 1877. When seen adhering to the black basalt of the chasms, the white waxy flowers, more like white hyacinths than orchids, make a beautiful contrast to the wilderness of the scene’. (part of Fitzgerald’s text accompanying Plate 10, Part 7, Volume 1, Australian Orchids, October 1882). Fitzgerald may have been mistaken as to which specimens were used to describe the species as they are more accurately attributed to those collected by Moore himself in 1860. For treatment on Lord Howe Island see also (Green 1994: 538).

This orchid is very popular in cultivation and has been selected and line bred to such an extent that most modern cultivated plants are of horticultural origin. Hybridises very rarely with Dendrobium discolor. A localised, compact-growing variant of Dendrobium phalaenopsis that occurs naturally in coastal ranges between Daintree and Cairns (mainly Macalister Range) was named by C.T. White in 1941 as Dendrobium phalaenopsis var. compactum and renamed Dendrobium bigibbum var. compactum (C.T.White) P.B.Adams (Adams 2018). It has short pseudobulbs 75--150 mm long, the shorter ones often conical in shape and usually has racemes with only 2 or 3 flowers, each 60--70 mm wide with a relatively narrow labellum. It grows on rocks, boulders and cliff faces on ridges and slopes where the plants are often exposed to full sun. It can withstand long periods of hot dry conditions during which the plants may completely defoliate. This compact variant was renamed at species rank in 1989 as Dendrobium lithocola, but this status is not supported by molecular studies. This variant, which has suffered severely from habitat destruction and illegal collecting, was once very popular in cultivation, but the distinctive compact habit is apparently a result of the harsh habitat and not genetic. Growers have noticed that the new pseudobulbs in cultivated plants were often longer than earlier ones and the plants eventually lost the distinctive compact habit and matched those from other areas.

The following have previously been recognised as distinct taxa and given formal botanical names, but are now informally grouped here as variants of Thelychiton speciosus subsp. curvicaulis. These variants are often difficult to define with certainty due to lack of genetic stability and the impact of hybridisation. Thelychiton pedunculatus (Clemesha) M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones: a localised dwarf variant that grows on rocks in exposed situations on western slopes between Mt Windsor Tableland and Evelyn Tableland in north-eastern Qld. Plants often have short tapered pseudobulbs, erect leaves, erect racemes with a long peduncle and each pseudobulb usually produces a single inflorescence from the apex. New growths are often stained with purple or dark red and the capsules are also purplish. Thelychiton spectabilis D.L.Jones & M.A.Clem.: a locally common variant that has long cylindrical pseudobulbs, racemes with a short, thick, ribbed peduncle and densely crowded, large, creamy yellow to pale yellow flowers. It occurs on mountains around Eungella, Qld, growing high on trees (also on cliffs and boulders) in rainforest and on sheltered slopes and near streams in tall open forest. Plants on trees form large, bulky clumps with an upright growth habit, those on rocks have shorter pseudobulbs that are swollen at base. Thelychiton biconvexus D.L.Jones & M.A.Clem.: a locally common variant that grows on rocks, cliff faces and trees in or close to rainforest on Mt Windsor Tableland, Big Tableland, Mt Amos and Mt Finnigan, north-eastern Qld. The pseudobulbs are straight or curved, spindle-shaped, ellipsoid in cross-section with sharp edges; the racemes have a long, slender, smooth peduncle and large, white or cream flowers. Thelychiton rupicola D.L.Jones & M.A.Clem.: a widespread and common variant that occurs on Mt Windsor Tableland and Atherton Tableland, extending south to Mt Elliot and possibly Sarina. The plants have relatively short, tapered pseudobulbs, and racemes with a long, slender, smooth peduncle and small flowers. It grows on boulders, escarpments and cliff faces, often in exposed situations. Plants from some areas have reddish new growth and young leaves.

Thelychiton capricornicus (Clemesha) M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones: a localised variant that has spreading roots, cylindrical pseudobulbs, arching to drooping racemes with a long peduncle and small, white flowers. It grows on rock faces of old volcanic plugs in central Qld (Byfield Range to Yeppoon and Rockhampton area). New growths are sometimes stained purplish. Thelychiton coriaceus D.L.Jones & M.A.Clem.: an inland variant that has spreading roots, relatively short tapered pseudobulbs, racemes with a slender, smooth peduncle and thick and fleshy, creamy yellow to yellow flowers. It grows on boulders, escarpments and cliff faces in central Qld (Blackdown Tableland, Carnarvon Gorge and Mt Moffat). New growths and young leaves are dark purple in colour. Thelychiton epiphyticus D.L.Jones & M.A.Clem.: a variant from the Illawarra region of N.S.W. (Robertson to Cambewarra) that grows on trees in tall, moist to wet forests, including rainforest, and around waterfalls and escarpments and on cliff faces. It has long, usually cylindrical pseudobulbs and racemes with a short, thick peduncle. Thelychiton rex (M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones) M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones: a common variant, spectacular when in flower, that has a mixture of erect, litter-trapping roots and spreading roots, short to long pseudobulbs that are usually cylindrical, racemes without an obvious peduncle and large, creamy yellow to bright yellow flowers. It is locally common in central and southern Qld (Mt Larcom/Calliope Range to Bunya Mountains/Conondale) growing on trees and rocks on ridges and slopes in rainforest and streamside vegetation. Plants growing on trees form large bulky clumps with an upright growth habit, whereas plants on rocks tend to have shorter pseudobulbs with a swollen base. Thelychiton tarberi (M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones) M.A.Clem. & D.L.Jones: a widespread and common variant that has erect, litter-trapping roots, cylindrical pseudobulbs, racemes without an obvious peduncle and small, white or cream flowers. It ranges from Maleny in Qld to Mangrove Mountain in N.S.W. and inland to Darling Downs, growing on trees and rocks in moist forest and rainforest, sometimes forming huge clumps several metres across. Plants from inland areas grow on rocks and have shorter pseudobulbs and fewer aerial roots.

Direct sequencing of the Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) region from two central tissue samples of root tubers from a specimen of this species from Theda Station (M.D. Barrett 4910, PERTH) returned two identical sequences of a Lactifluus (Pers.) Roussel (Russulaceae; GenBank record ON819578). This suggests that the primary endophytes of Dipodium ammolithum are Russulaceae, in agreement with previous findings (Bougoure & Dearnaley 2005, Dearnaley & Le Brocque 2006, Boddington et al. 2016). A third tuber tissue sample (GenBank ON819579) sequenced from this same Dipodium specimen belonged to the genus Clitopilus (Entolomataceae; e.g. 97.4 % BLAST match to Clitopilus prunulus EU273512). Species of Clitopilus are usually considered saprophytes, but C. hobsonii (Berk.) P.D.Orton has recently been recorded as a root symbiont of Liquidambar (Peng et al. 2021). The presence of Clitopilus in this Dipodium sample is most likely incidental, but the possibility of a symbiotic interaction cannot be excluded.

First discovered near Albany, W.A., in 1944. At the time it was believed to be an Australian native which H.M.R. Rupp described in 1946 as Monadenia australiensis. Its exotic status was later recognised, and it is now known to have colonised large tracts of land. The circumstances surrounding the introduction of this orchid to Australia remain a mystery, however the seeds may well have arrived mixed in with stock fodder imported from South Africa after the Boer War. It is a significant pest that has successfully spread over a wide area of southern Australia. Because it mainly grows on disturbed or degraded sites, it has had limited impact on native orchids. It has more recently colonised tracts of land in Vic. and Tas.

This species was once abundant on the basalt plains immediately N and W of Melbourne. They were so common that flowers were collected annually by a staff member of the Botany department at Melbourne University and distributed to students for floral dissection. As a student of Agricultural Science at the time, I was one of the lucky ones to dissect and draw some of these flowers. This practice stopped in the 1960s when sufficient numbers of flowers were not available for collection. While at the University Field Station at Derrimut near Deer Park in 1966 I visited the railway site at Tottenham and walked all the railway lines in the area looking for orchids. Living plants of Diuris fragrantissima (then known as D. punctata var. albo-violacea) were located in 1965 and 1966 at Tottenham Sanctuary, Sunshine railway yards near main set of points, St Albans, Stony Creek, Deer Park and Sydenham. At the Stony Creek site I made the note ‘plants on last legs, no future at this site.’ Weeds, particularly rye grass, wild oats, fog grass, sweet vernal grass and thistles, were impacting significantly on many parts of the railway reserves. About this time the herbicide Simazine was used to control weeds on the railway tracks and spraydrift killed or damaged numerous native plants along the reserves, including plants of Diuris fragrantissima at Sunshine railway yards, causing stunted growth and abnormal variegated patterns in the leaves. Annual monitoring of the sites showed worsening weed infestations and fewer and fewer orchid plants and it was obvious that the species had little chance of survival in the wild without a helping hand. In hope I sent wild-collected seed to Mark Clements at the Australian National Botanic Gardens in Canberra in 1976 and he successfully raised seedlings using the symbiotic method of germination. Seedlings were grown at the ANBG and also distributed to Victorian members of the Australian Native Orchid Society. These plants provided an impetus for the conservation of the species.

Plants of Dockrillia linguiformis can survive in extremely exposed situations, including north and west facing positions on dark cliff faces and rocks. In very dry seasons the leaves can shrivel significantly, but usually fatten again after substantial rains. The flowers are pollinated by female workers of small native bees in family Colletidae, subfamily Euryglossinae (Jones 1974). 2 species were identified in the study, Euryglossina hypochroma and E. lynettae. The bees, attracted to the flowering plants on warm days by the floral perfume and massed racemes, enter a flower and probe the base of the column and labellum with their mouthparts extended, gaining purchase by footholds on the labellum callus. Glue from the rostellum is smeared on the insect’s thorax on entry to the flower and on exiting, the insect contacts finger-like projections on the anther cap which pivots, sliding the pollinia neatly onto the patch of glue. Deposition occurs on the stigma when entering another flower.

This is a very hardy species that can survive on boulders and cliff faces exposed to hot, westerly summer sun. In very dry seasons the leaves can shrivel significantly, but usually fatten again after substantial rains. A pollination study revealed female native bees (Hylaeus (Gnathoprosopsis) albonitens - family Colletidae) to be effective pollinators (Bartareau 1999) above 20˚C. The bees are attracted to the nectarless flowers on warm days by a sweet perfume. The bees land on the flower, move to the labellum, often scratching on the calli, and enter the flower, receiving a coating of sticky stigmatic fluid on the thorax in the process. While struggling to leave the flower the pollinium is deposited on the sticky patch on the insect’s thorax. Deposition of the pollinia on the stigma occurs when visiting a second flower.

This species, together with Dendrobium canaliculatum and D. discolor, was first collected in Australia by the Swedish naturalist Dr Daniel Carl Solander in 1770. Solander was one of the scientists on board Captain Cook’s barque Endeavour when it was careened on the bank of what is now the Endeavour River (the vicinity of present day Cooktown, north-eastern Qld) after a damaging encounter with coral on the Great Barrier Reef. Dockrillia rigida, which was among the scientific specimens he collected, was sketched by the natural history artist Sydney Parkinson who was also on the ship. His sketch was later prepared as a coloured botanical engraving that was used in Banks’ Florilegium, a set of botanical engravings of plants collected on Captains Cook’s first voyage. The sketch would have also been of significant assistance to Robert Brown when he described Dendrobium rigidum in 1810. Hybridises with Dockrillia fasciculata (see Dockrillia ×foederata).

The Indian taxon Habenaria foliosa var. foetida has a remarkably similar growth habit and floral features to H. hymenophylla and the flowers of both have a strong, foetid odour. Wallace (1974) wrote a detailed study of the pollination of this species by flesh flies (family Sarcophagidae). The flies land on the labellum and feed on the nectar, moving progressively further into the flower until they becomes trapped between the column and the labellum. On backing out after struggling free, the insect’s back is smeared with glue from the rostellum, the anther cap is dislodged by contact and the pollinia then drops onto the smeared patch. Pollen deposition occurs during a visit to a second flower when the pollinia become wedged onto the stigma.

Plants with green or yellowish green flowers are not uncommon among populations, but plants with short, bract-like leaves and unusually small, green flowers occur in swampy, near-coastal areas of N.S.W. (these plants are very similar to Orthoceras strictum forma viride Hatch from New Zealand). Very robust plants with large, dark brown to black flowers with an elongated labellum midlobe occur in dense swamps in the Otway region, Vic. Attracted by dull floral colours, scent and nectar, the beetles gather on the inflorescence and probe the flowers to gather nectar, picking up pollinaria on the face and antennae. Wallace (1980) reported the pollination of Peristeranthus hilli by species of click beetle, Agonischius australis, (family Elateridae) and an unidentified species of net-winged beetle, Metriorrhynchus (family Lycidae). His observations were made on cultivated plants growing outside the natural range of the orchid. Further pollination observations of this orchid, this time in the wild near Boonah, south-eastern Qld, established the identity of the second beetle as M. rufipennis (Forster 1988) by matching a drawing of the beetle in Wallace’s paper. Beetles are clumsy vectors and mostly inefficient pollinators, however, it is common to see large numbers of capsules on this orchid suggesting some other vector or mechanism is involved in its pollination.

Originally recorded as locally abundant at Gorae West near Portland from ‘Flat, heavily timbered country, rather rough, in black loam soil.’ The species is now highly localised and known from only 2 sites; near Condah it grows among rushes and tussocks in and around the margins of a swamp in water, whereas near Dunkeld it grows in wet grassland and grassy woodland; found growing in seasonally wet, heavy, dark grey to black loam.

Nicholls emphasised the floral variation of this orchid when he first described the species: ‘The new species is probably one of the most variable, in regard to the floral characters on record.’ (Nicholls 1942). There are morphological differences between the 2 surviving populations, but floral variation makes them difficult to separate and a molecular study showed there was little genetic difference between the populations. Cliff Beauglehole provided some interesting historical notes to W.H. Nicholls about the type locality of this orchid. ‘During the winter months the area of several hundred acres (known locally as ‘Malseeds’), where this orchid flourishes, is covered to a depth of 2 or more feet of water; really it is a wide creek bed, a natural watercourse; a favourite feeding ground for emus and kangaroos. The fact that the season 1941 was the driest for 25 years probably explains why this orchid had not been recorded before.’ (Nicholls 1942).

The identity of P. fuscum has been contentious. Examination by the author of flower from the type specimen of P. fuscum showed that the labellum shape was very similar to that of P. uroglossum and on this basis the latter was treated as synonym of P. fuscum (Jones 2000). However closer examination of both taxa produced a different result. In both species the labellum is broadest near the base and constricted above the middle, ending in a tapered tail-like portion. The labellum of P. fuscum is however smaller (5--6 mm long) than that of P. uroglossum (8--9 mm) and with a significantly shorter tail-like extension (c. 2 mm long compared to c. 4.5 mm long in P. uroglossum). The confusion between these 2 species exemplifies the complexities within this group of orchids which contains many species that have a restricted distribution and grow in specialised habitats (Jones 2000).

Known only from a single locality; found growing among grass tussocks and forbs on low mounds surrounded by seasonally inundated depressions in disturbed River Red Gum woodland in heavy clay soil. The landform where this species grows is known as 'gilgai' or 'crabhole country' which develops on heavy clay that cracks when dry and swells when wet. Detritus falling into the racks adds to the volume of material which, when wet, swells and forms irregular mounds that become surrounded by sunken potholes and crabholes which fill with water. The orchids do not actually grow in water, but on mounds of saturated soil.
Vic. (NE near Benalla); c. 170 m altitude.

This species, which has a long flowering period of 4 to 5 months, is also morphologically variable. Northern populations generally flower earlier than plants in southern areas, but early- and late-flowering populations also occur in some localities. A striking colour variation occurs on some granite outcrops in the wheat belt, the whole plants being a deep red colour. South coast populations, found growing on stabilised dunes, are generally slender with a few pale flowers and can be easily confused with Prasophyllum calcicola. Populations in some inland areas have longer-than-usual antenna-like tips on the lateral sepals.

A remarkable orchid that can be very difficult to see because of its lowly stature and cryptic flowers. The rosette leaves are usually withered by flowering time. Although the flowers project outwards from the flower stem with pedicels and ovaries more or less held horizontally, the pedicels change after pollination and seed capsules are held erect to facilitate seed dispersal. This species was first collected in September 1803 by Scottish botanist Robert Brown from the roadside ‘between Parramatta and Green Hills’ in an area of N.S.W. at the time known as Port Jackson. It was also collected a month later in October 1803 by English botanist and collector George Caley from an area known by him as ‘Cowpastures’, located on the Cumberland Plain near Sydney. Caley prepared detailed descriptions in his diary of various species he collected and referred to Pterostylis as ‘Druids Caps’, applying the tag name ‘Druid’s Cap Brownii’ to this species (Webb & Lister 1991). Brown used the specimens he collected in September as the basis for his naming and description of the species. The type sheet of P. gibbosa, held at the British Museum of Natural History, also contains specimens of P. saxicola (see also that species entry). Pollinated by sexually deceived, tiny, fat-bodied male gnats in family Sciaridae. This small, distinctive orchid has a puzzling distribution. It's mainly a coastal species throughout its range, however, a disjunct inland and high-altitude population occurs in the Daves Creek area of the McPherson Range, south-eastern Qld. Here it grows in a highly specialised plant community known as Mountain Mallee Heath at about 900 m altitude, surrounded by tall forest. This plant community covers roughly 160 hectares and consists of mallee eucalypts and low, heathy plants growing in loam and peaty soil derived from volcanic rocks in an open area exposed to strong sunlight and strong winds. Other specialised orchids grow here, including Calochilus grandiflorus and Corunastylis sigmoidea. A small, isolated population of Pterostylis pedoglossa also grows on the western side of the central tablelands of N.S.W., 150 km from the coast.
Found in a wide range of habitats, some species extending well inland.

Qld (Daves Creek area, Lamington Plateau), N.S.W. (Nelson Bay to Green Cape, Blue Mountains, disjunct population in W parts of central tablelands in Lithgow-Wolgan Valley area), Vic. (E of Melbourne in S), Tas. (SE, E, N, Cape Barren Island); 5--900 m altitude.

Belongs to a complex group of orchids which includes many distinctive species that are readily recogniseable by morphological features, and others which are much harder to define and can be quite variable. Vegetative features, including presence or absence of a basal rosette of leaves, number of cauline leaves on the flower stem and presence of hair-like siliceous cells on the stems, ovary and leaf margins, can be very useful characters for classification. Shape and size of the labellum and ‘hairiness’ of the labellum margins are also important. The development of apical thickening or clubbing (instead of filamentous tips) on the free points of the lateral sepals is also a useful floral feature. Commonly known as snail orchids because of the shape of their small, neat, pillarbox-like, hooded flower, they grow in vegetative colonies and have similar flowering and non-flowering plants with the flower stem arising from the centre of the rosette. The dorsal sepal and petals are mostly of similar length. The front of the flower is tightly enclosed by erect, fused sepals with no lateral gap and short to long, filamentous or thickened free points. The short labellum is totally hidden within the flower and has a curved, lobed or brush-like basal appendage. Pollination seems to be mainly by male gnats of the family Sciaridae. For further information, see Jones (1998), Jones & Clements (2002a-d), Jones & French (2014a-d; 2015; 2017).

Often forms extensive, dense, clonal colonies with a high proportion of flowering plants in wet years. It colonises decaying logs and the upper parts of trunks of living or dead tree ferns in wet forests and fern gullies. The author observed and collected gnats (Acrodicrania species, family Mycetophilidae) pollinating flowers in a colony at Montrose, Vic., in October 1973. Several gnats were seen flying around the flowers on a cool, humid day and were observed to enter the orchid flowers through the lateral gap between the edge of the synsepalum and the margin of the petals. Gnats carrying yellow pollinia were also observed entering other flowers. Although the gnats often entered the flowers through the lateral gap they usually emerged from the flower through the frontal opening. The gnats were only inside the flowers for a few minutes.

A detailed pollination study of this species in south-western Australia (Phillips et al. 2014), showed it was pollinated by males of a single species of fungus gnat in the genus Mycoma (family Mycetophilidae). Of 135 gnats observed to visit flowers, all but 2 alighted on the labellum, but only a very low proportion (13 insects) triggered the labellum and of these only 6 insects became trapped in the flower. Trapped insects were in the flower from 1 to 7 minutes and were observed to fly while inside the flower. Copulatory movements of the abdomen were seen while the insects were on the labellum. Some insects also landed on closed labella that had already been triggered.

The rosettes emerge first in autumn and the inflorescences develop in spring. The rosettes actually develop from the parent (old) tuber and the flower stem is produced from the new replacement tuber, while both tubers are still connected. In all other species of "Speculantha" the rosette arises after flowering and is borne on a lateral growth from the base of the flower stem, often after flowering is finished. The rosettes of S. vernalis are always present at flowering time and new rosettes can subsequently develop on lateral growths which arise from the base of the inflorescence. The spring flowering period is also notable since related species flower in summer, autumn and early winter. Flowering is promoted in the season following summer fires.

It flowers en masse after hot summer fires, rarely without fires; sometimes a few plants flower after mowing or slashing. The author observed small native bees visiting flowers at Anglesea, Vic., and witnessed the removal and deposition of pollinia. The bees entered the flower headfirst via the labellum and completely disappeared inside the tube between the labellum and column. Rhizanthella gardneri is a rare subterranean orchid which lacks chlorophyll and lives in association with a mycorrhizal fungus and the roots of a broombush. The main section of its rhizome grows forwards about 10 cm below ground level and progressively dies off behind. Lateral branches are formed which grow horizontally through the soil. Each branch is ultimately terminated by an inflorescence and prior to flowering the apex of the rhizome turns at right angles and grows towards the soil surface, ending in an inflorescence (flowerhead or capitulum). The overlapping sterile bracts of the inflorescence are incurved over the flowers while the flowerhead is still buried, keeping the flowers free of soil. These bracts reflex back quickly when a flowerhead is exposed above ground, the position apparent in most published photos of this species. Flowering in the capitulum lasts about three weeks and a high proportion of the flowers produce seed. After the seeds have matured, the branch dies. Careful excavation of flowering plants has revealed links to the decayed growths of previous years, and it is reasonable to presume that all of the orchid plants growing in close proximity are of clonal origin. The flowerheads of this orchid often raise slight bumps in the soil surface and sometimes cracks or holes appear where the tips of the floral bracts protrude through the soil and leaf litter. Individual flowers face the centre of the flowerhead and are arranged in a series of spirals extending out from the centre. Each flower remains open for several days and exudes a faint, sweet scent in warm weather. They are visited by a suite of insects including small flies, wasps and termites. Termites may be involved in the orchid’s pollination (Dixon et al. 1990), but the main pollinator is a small species of humpback fly or scuttle fly (family Phoridae) which has been observed on a few occasions carrying a pollinarium on its thorax (photos page 398, Brundrett 2014). After pollination the seeds take about seven months to mature. There is no elongation of the flower stem during this time and the seeds mature below ground level. At maturity the fruit is yellowish and fleshy. It is unique among orchids being a drupe (not a capsule) that does not split to release the seeds (20--150 per fruit). The seeds themselves are unusually large for an orchid and with a hard sclerotic coat. Warcup (1985) showed that the seeds can germinate in the absence of the mycorrhizal fungus to form a protocorm, but further growth ceases unless the protocorm is invaded by the mycorrhizal fungus which enters through the protocorm hairs.

All sites of Rhizanthella gardneri discovered to date have an annual rainfall of 300--400 mm per annum which falls mainly in winter. Vegetation types include mallee heath, mallee scrub and, less commonly, woodland. The dominant shrubs in these communities are species of broombush (Melaleuca hamata, M. scalena and M. uncinata) which grow in extensive thickets. Rhizanthella gardneri is usually found in thickets of M. scalena, growing near creek lines. The vast majority (if not all) of the orchid plants discovered to date have been growing within 10--30 cm of a living broombush lignotuber at a depth of about 10 cm. The soils are mainly freely draining, sandy clay or sandy loam that become yellow with depth.
W.A. (Babakin, Goomalling Moonigin, Shackleton, Corrigin and Wubin); c. 300 m altitude.

This remarkable orchid was discovered on 23 May 1928 by John Trott while ploughing an area of rolled mallee some 16 km SE of Corrigin. Its discovery and the subsequent erection of a new genus in Orchidaceae with a totally subterranean life cycle aroused tremendous interest in the botanical world (Rogers 1928, Wilson 1929). In all Trott uncovered around 36 plants at this site. Seven more sightings were made up until 1960, all being accidental discoveries of a similar nature. In 1979 living plants were discovered at Munglinup (some 300 km SE of the original site). Recent morphological and molecular studies have shown this population to be a separate and distinct species (see Rhizanthella johnstonii). Detailed studies, financed by the World Wildlife Fund Australia and the Australian Orchid Foundation, were carried out by Kingsley Dixon and John Pate. These researchers were ably assisted by members of the Western Australian Native Orchid Study and Conservation Group (WANOS) who carried out detailed searches of promising sites. These studies enjoyed spectacular success and more than 150 plants of the orchid were discovered in five sites from 1980--82 (Dixon & Pate 1984). Researchers have made astounding strides in their knowledge of the western underground orchids since the discovery of the Munglinup specimens in 1979, however, many questions still remain unanswered. In particular the method of seed dispersal remains unknown although the succulent nature of the mature fruit suggests that they are probably distributed in animal dung after being eaten by truffle-seeking bandicoots or potoroos. The observation by Alex George, that freshly cut tissue of the orchid emits a smell like that of formalin is intriguing and may aid detection of the ripe fruit. The rapid reflexing of the floral bracts on flower heads that have been exposed by excavation is also interesting.

Most of the details of the biology of this species, which is very similar to that outlined for Rhizanthella gardneri, have come from the research carried out by Mark Clements for the Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research in Canberra. Mark has kindly made the results of his studies freely available for my use. Plants of R. slateri can occur singly, but most often form clumps comprising single or conjoined rhizomes at a depth of 20--25 cm underground. Growth occurs all year round, but fluctuates in response to rain. Plants occur in various stages of development with new and old growths present on the same plant. Rhizomes consist of a series of internodes with meristematic buds at the nodes, each subtended by a small bract. New lateral rhizomes arise from these buds. The basal area where it is attached to the parent rhizome is only a few millimeters wide, but older parts reach 10--15 mm across. The narrow basal connection is easily broken, but separated parts can develop individually. Excavations of several plants revealed an interconnected labyrinth of multiple decaying, mature, developing and immature rhizomes up to 25 cm apart at the furthest points. In one case up to 27 individual rhizomes (plants) were found in an area of about 250 cm2. Rhizomes first develop laterally, flowering when large enough. Prior to flowering, the apex of the largest rhizomes grow towards the soil surface, taking 4 to 6 months before developing a capitulum that just emerges at the soil surface under the litter layer, anytime between January and October. Flowering occurs from August to early November. The capitulum, which is slightly funnel-shaped, consists of an outer layer of sterile sheathing bracts and a series of spirally arranged individual flowers (up to 30), each subtended by a floral bract. Individual flowers are tubular, creamy white, maturing to pink, red or maroon with the sepals and petals held close together, the triangular labellum protruding between them. Rhizanthella slateri is pollinated by small microdipterans (gnats), possibly attracted by a mushroom-like odour. They enter the open flower, possibly deceived into laying eggs or seeking nectar, and pick up a pollinarium on the thorax when leaving the flower. Deposition on the stigma occurs when visiting another flower. The percentage of pollination observed in flowerheads is unusually high (70--100%), indicating an efficient system and a strong attraction for the pollinators. Self-pollination has been ruled out because cultivated plants grown out of their natural habitat do not produce capsules. Pollinated flowers develop into fleshy, indehiscent drupes that take 11--12 months to mature. At first the cream-coloured ovaries develop below the ground surface, enlarging to a cluster of fleshy, yellow, aromatic drupes at or near the soil surface but under the litter layer. The ripe berry-like fruit contain dark brown sclerotic seeds, 16--900 per fruit. Seed dispersal is probably by truffle-eating animals such as swamp wallabies and bandicoots feeding on the ripe fruit, or birds such as choughs and bower birds, the seeds passing through the gut and being dispersed in dung. The impact of a bushfire at Alum Mountain showed that Rhizanthella flowerheads covered by thick litter were destroyed, eliminating seed production for that year, but the rhizomes, which were more deeply buried, regrew below the damaged tissue.

In stark contrast with Western Australia's Rhizanthella gardneri, this eastern species occurs in areas with a high and reliable rainfall; Bulahdelah for example, where most of the research on R. slateri has been carried out, has an annual rainfall of c. 1350 mm per annum. R. slateri is found in a range of forested habitats all of which include shrubs and trees in the family Myrtaceae, particularly open forest and woodland with species of Angophora, Corymbia, Eucalyptus, Leptospermum and Melaleuca. Other diverse habitats include wet sclerophyll forest, littoral rainforest and streambank vegetation with species of Syncarpia and Tristaniopsis. Soils are mostly freely draining sand or loam. Apart from the general importance of myrtaceous plants, no tree or shrub species forms a common link between the localities.

N.S.W. (localised and disjunct: Agnes Banks, Heaton State Forest near Newcastle, Bulahdelah, near Nabiac, Hazelbrook, Katoomba, Turramurra, Nowra/Jervis Bay, Springwood, Wentworth Falls, Wisemans Ferry, Woollamia); 10--400 m altitude.

Much of the early history of this orchid presented here is based on material from Lionel Gilbert’s fascinating book The Orchid Man (Gilbert 1992), which all orchid lovers should read. Cryptanthemis slateri was discovered in November 1931 on the lower western slopes of Alum Mountain, Bulahdelah, in north-central coastal N.S.W. by Ernest William Slater when he was digging up a plant or plants of a Dipodium for friends (probably D. variegatum which is common in the area). Slater thought the ‘curious object might be of orchidaceous character’ and sent the specimen together with the Dipodium plants to Mr & Mrs Frederick J. Fieldsend of East Maitland who were friends with the Reverend Herman Rupp, a noted orchid authority in N.S.W. at the time. Although the flowers were withered, Rupp realized it was an orchid and recognised its similarity to Rhizanthella gardneri which had been discovered in W.A. some three years earlier. A very excited Rupp immediately contacted Slater and within a week 4 more specimens were found. These were used by Rupp as type material to erect the genus Cryptanthemis and formally name the species as Cryptanthemis slateri (Rupp 1932); he later provided more details of the species in another paper (Rupp 1934). The discovery of this orchid created much excitement in the eastern Australian botanical community and many people looked for the novelty, often digging up Dipodium plants while searching. Such was the interest in the underground species that Rupp observed ‘So much interest has been aroused by Cryptanthemis that I tremble for the welfare of Dipodium, which is a beautiful thing.’ Rupp visited Bulahdelah in 1933 and photographed a partly excavated plant of the orchid in situ. An article on the species with 2 full pages of photos was included in the Australian Orchid Review for June 1938.

Locally common, extending from coastal districts to adjacent ranges; found growing on shrubs and trees, occasionally on rocks and boulders, in positions exposed to moderate or strong air movement in a range of humid, moist to wet habitats. Found beside small streams, creeks, gorges and waterfalls in open forest, coastal streams and estuaries, slopes above sheltered gullies and fern gullies in tall, wet forest and sparse, drier types of rainforest and thickets. It often grows on regrowth following disturbances and where there are breaks in the forest canopy such as stream banks, logged areas, tracks and beside roads. Sarcochilus australis grows on wide range of shrubs and trees, sometimes high up in the canopy, but often on trunks and main branches at eye-level, sometimes even closer to the ground. It also frequently grows as a twig epiphyte on thin stems and twigs of the outer canopy of shrubs and trees, sometimes hanging by just a couple of roots. Dislodged plants are commonly found on ground after storms. Frequent host plants in N.S.W. are Water Gum, which commonly grows beside streams, Eastern Leatherwood and Grey Myrtle, both forming thickets on dry, but humid, slopes and gullies. The largest plants are found in Vic. and Tas., where the flowers are often wholly green with a contrasting white labellum. Frequent hosts in Vic. and/or Tas. include Hazel (Pomaderris aspera), Dogwood (Pomaderris apetala), Austral Mulberry (Hedycarya angustifolia), Water Gum, Musk Daisy-bush (Olearia argophylla), Blanket Leaf (Bedfordia arborescens), Christmas Bush (Prostanthera lasianthos), Lilly Pilly (Syzygium smithii), Myrtle Beech, Varnish Wattle (Acacia verniciflua), Blackwood, Tree Violet (Melicytus dentatus) and Prickly Currant (Coprosma quadrifida). N.S.W. (Kyogle, near Tenterfield, Glen Innes, Dorrigo Plateau to Nadgee), Vic. (S areas sporadically W from Howe Ranges to Otway Ranges), Tas. (E, central N, NE and NW, Flinders Island, Cape Barren Island); 0--1000 m altitude. Although widely distributed, this orchid is absent from Qld and generally rare and disjunct in the northern part of range where it occurs at higher altitudes than in southern areas. Its much more common in the southern part of its range, particularly in Tas., where it has been recorded growing very close to sea level in the north-west.

Plants from N.S.W. tend to be smaller than those from southerly states and can flower while they are quite small; the sepals and petals are brownish and the labellum and column are often strongly marked with colour. These plants match the taxon described as Gunnia picta, named in 1838 by John Lindley based on specimens grown in England which were originally ‘from the neighbourhood of Sydney’. For an excellent summary of the status of this orchid in Tas., see Smith (2008).

A very widespread and common species that occurs in a wide range of habitats from near sea level on the coast, to high in the mountains, usually where there is plenty of air movement. In southern parts of its range it extends from the lowlands to high in the mountains, but in the tropics it's restricted to mountains and tablelands above c. 500 m altitude. It's often prominent on trees growing on exposed slopes and ridge tops where breezes, mists, clouds and drizzly weather are frequent, but it also occurs in gullies, near streams and on sheltered, humid slopes, often in or near rainforest, but also other moist to wet forests. Also occurs in small isolated patches of humid coastal forest near estuaries and behind large dunes. Perhaps surprisingly, it sometimes grows on river oaks beside streams in fairly open, but humid, situations and is known to colonise relict trees left in cleared paddocks, cultivated fruit trees and other garden trees and shrubs. It grows on rocks, trunks and larger branches of a wide range of shrubs and trees. Large wattles are a common host, particularly Blackwood growing along ridges where humid air drains; other hosts include Red Cedar, Antarctic Beech, Myrtles (Austromyrtus and Backhousia species), Sassafras (Doryphora sassafras), Lilly Pillies (Syzygium species), Figs (Ficus species), Swamp Mahogany, Stinging Trees (Dendrocnide species), Water Gums, Brush Box, Bolwarra (Eupomatia laurina) and Eastern Leatherwood. It has also been found at high altitudes growing on Banksia monticola (David Banks pers. comm.).

This is the most widely distributed species of Sarcochilus and also the most common. Being such a widely distributed species, this orchid exhibits significant variation in flowering time, plant habit, floral morphology and fragrance (see also S. niveus). Variable morphological features include flower size, tepal size and shape, labellum size, shape of the lateral lobes, blunt or pointed apex on the labellum midlobe, and patterns of colour on the labellum. Walsh (1998) draws attention to a variant with light to heavy purple striations and other marks on the labellum apex (sometimes solid purple), strong mustard yellow colouration on the lateral lobes and an intense vanilla-like fragrance. He records this variant as occurring between Dorrigo Plateau and Barrington Tops at around 600 m altitude, but it also occurs as far south as Robertson in the southern tablelands at around 730 m. Some plants with a pinkish blush to the flowers have been found at Dorrigo, N.S.W. and Kroombit Tops, Qld. Floral perfumes vary from a strong, sweet, spicy fragrance to resembling that of orange-blossom or vanilla essence or simply unpleasant. Aerial growths can develop on aborted racemes. For an inspired treatise and lovely photos of Sarcochilus falcatus see Walsh (1998).

Fitzgerald (1888) studied the pollination of Spiranthes australis in the vicinity of Sydney, the type location for the species, and concluded that the pollinia were so tightly encased in the anther that they could not be extracted and the flowers were self-pollinating - in his very unusual and descriptive wording ‘in my opinion it is never made fruitful by the pollen from another flower.’ However, the self-pollination process in these central N.S.W. plants is not straightforward because there is no obvious rostellum separating the anther and the stigma and the pollen grains do not simply fall onto the stigma or come into contact with its upper surface. It is quite possible these plants are apomictic. By contrast, plants from some areas have functional pollinia attached to a removable viscidium and are probably insect-pollinated; in others the viscidium is abortive meaning that the pollinarium cannot be extracted from the flowers as a unit. Flowers of this latter type can also have loosely packed, friable pollinia and are commonly either self-pollinating via the pollen falling onto the stigma, or apomictic. Insect-pollinated flowers of S. australis are often visited by small, dark, native bees which work their way upward on the spikes, probing deep into the flowers for nectar and during the process picking up pollinia on the face around the mouthparts. This species varies considerably in flower size and degree of spotting. There are self-pollinating variants (usually with smaller flowers that open only on very hot days and often for brief periods) and insect-pollinated variants which have large, long-lasting flowers that are often scented and open readily on warm to hot days. Although generally associated with spotted flowers, it is not uncommon to find plants of this orchid with unspotted flowers. Hybrids occur with many other sun orchids including Thelymitra antennifera, T. azurea and T. mucida; also with T. carnea and/or T. rubra (see T. ×irregularis) and with members of the T. nuda-T. pauciflora complexes (see T. ×truncata and T. ×merraniae). The flowers of these hybrids are usually spotted.
